2.
Learned counsel for the applicants contends that the respondent no.2 approached the Police Authority by way of an FIR which is contained in Annexure-P/5.

Their marriage was settled with the consent of families of applicant as well as respondent no.2.
The applicant used to come to the house of the complainant and the complainant also used to visit the applicant's house at Seoni.
On account of certain problem in families of both the applicant and respondent no.2, the marriage could not be solemnized.
Their engagement was held on 23.01.2020 and before engagement, with the consent of applicant and respondent no.2, they had physical relationship on 12.02.2016.
Thereafter, on many occasions they had physical relationship.

Later on, the father of the complainant expired and parents of applicant also expired and then the present applicant made a call to the mother of complainant and expressed that he was not willing to enter into wedlock with the complainant, as his late parents were not happy with the relationship.
3. It is contended by the counsel that the FIR has been lodged under Section 376(2)(n) of IPC and to attract the provisions of aforesaid section there has to be false promise.
In the present case, there was no question of any false promise as admittedly the applicant and respondent no.2 came in touch through a matrimonial site.
Their families were also met with each other.

Their marriage was also settled even the engagement also took place, therefore, it is not a case where there was any false promise of marriage under garb of which, the present applicant behoved the respondent no.2 to enter in sexual intercourse.
4. It is contended by the counsel that such eventualities have been taken note of by the Apex Court in the case of Pramod Suryabhan Pawar vs. State of Maharashtra (2019 9 SCC 608).

sentences.text: In the present case, the complainant approached the police with a report which is contained in Annexure-P/6.
A perusal of report reflects that the applicant as well as respondent no.2 came in touch through a matrimonial site in the year 2015.
As per the FIR, the families of both the applicant and respondent no.2 met with each other.
Their marriage was fixed and even the engagement was also held.
10. A perusal of FIR reflects that as there were some problem in both the the families, the marriage could not be solemnized earlier.

It is further evident that respondent no.2 had physical relationship with the applicant at her house on 12.02.2016 and thereafter they had physical relationship on number of occasions as distinguished in the FIR.
However, the entire FIR nowhere prima facie suggests that there was any false promise of marriage.
11. Section 376(2)(n) of IPC came up for consideration before the Apex Court in the case of Pramod Suryabhan Pawar(supra).

The Apex Court while dealing with the issue, held in Pramod Suryabhan Pawar (supra) as under:
"Where the promise to marry is false and the intention of the maker at the time of making the promise itself was not to abide by it but to deceive the woman to convince her to engage in sexual relations, there is a "misconception of fact" that vitiates the woman's "consent".
On the other hand, a breach of a promise cannot be said to be a false promise.
To establish a false promise, the maker of the promise should have had no intention of upholding his word at the time of giving it.
The "consent" of a woman under Section 375 is vitiated on the ground of a "misconception of fact" where such misconception was the basis for her choosing to engage in the said act.

In Deepak Gulati [Deepak Gulati v.
State of Haryana, (2013) 7 SCC 675."

sentences.text: There is no allegation to the effect that the promise to marry given to the second respondent was false at the inception.

On the contrary, it would appear from the contents of the FIR that there was a subsequent refusal on the part of the appellant to marry the second respondent which gave rise to the registration of the FIR.

On these facts, we are of the view that the High Court was in error in declining to entertain the petition under Section 482CrPC on the basis that it was only the evidence at trial which would lead Abhshek Deshbhartar vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 15 May, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/115297663/

sentences.text: If this material, which is a part of the investigation papers, is perused carefully, it is obvious that the physical relationship between the appellant and the second respondent was consensual, at least from 2013 to 2017.
The fact that they were engaged was admitted by the second respondent.
The fact that in 2011, the appellant proposed her and in 2017, there was engagement is accepted by the second respondent.
In fact, she participated in the engagement ceremony without any protest.
However, she has denied that her marriage was solemnised with the appellant.
Taking the prosecution case as correct, it is not possible to accept that the second respondent maintained a physical relationship only because the appellant had given a promise of marriage.
14. Thus, if the allegations so levelled in the FIR are subjected to penetrating scrutiny, the same would reveal that in the entire FIR there are no allegations of false promise of marriage.

On the contrary, the complainant herself admitted in the FIR as both the families had some problem,
therefore, their marriage could not be solemnized.
It is thus, clear that it was not a case, where the consent was given by the respondent no.2 under misconception.
On the contrary, at the most it could have been treated to be a breach of promise but the same cannot be termed as false promise.

As neither FIR in its entire reading nor the statement under Section 164 of Cr.P.C or the statement of the witnesses reflect that there was any false promise of marriage by the present applicant,
therefore, this Court is of the considered view that in view of the law laid down by the Apex Court in the aforesaid decisions, no case under Section 376(2)(n) could have been registered.

15. Accordingly, this Court is of the considered view that the proceedings instituted against the applicant on the basis of FIR are unsustainable as the act in question do not attract the provisions of Section 376(2)(n) of IPC.
1 6 .
Resultantly, this petition is allowed.
The FIR and the ensued proceedings so far as it relates to applicant stand quashed.
The applicant is discharged from the aforesaid charges.

Bail bonds, if any,
furnished by the applicant stand discharged.
